title: Argument Evaluation in Verbal Problems
tagline: Year 3 — Judging the quality of arguments: fallacies, relevance, evidence, points at issue and principles

introduction.overview: Argument evaluation asks you to judge reasoning as a whole: whether a reply answers the point, which statement is irrelevant, what two speakers actually disagree about, which argument is most convincing, and which common fallacy a piece of reasoning commits. It extends the strengthen-weaken skills by naming the errors, so that you can recognise them quickly in new contexts.
introduction.placementRelevance: These items appear in the verbal sections of management and campus tests.
introduction.realWorldContext: Weighing a proposal in a meeting or a claim in an advertisement uses the same skills.

learningObjectives: Name common fallacies (ad hominem, straw man, false dilemma, circularity, slippery slope)
Find the point at issue between two speakers
Choose the argument with the best evidence
Identify the role of a statement in an argument

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A good argument has relevant, true premises and a conclusion that follows from them.

coreDefinitions: Ad hominem: attacking the person instead of the argument.
Straw man: misrepresenting a position so that it is easy to attack.
False dilemma: presenting only two options when more exist.
Circular reasoning: using the conclusion as a premise.
Slippery slope: claiming a chain of consequences without evidence.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Ask what the argument proves, what it assumes, and what it leaves out. A fallacy is a systematic way of failing at one of these.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Identify the conclusion, the premises, and the move from one to the other. Then ask which fallacy label, if any, describes the move.

mainNarrative: "Dr Rao's report on pollution cannot be trusted because he once failed an examination." The argument attacks the person rather than the report, which is an ad hominem fallacy.
"We must either ban all cars from the city or accept constant traffic jams." There are other options such as better public transport or congestion charges, so this is a false dilemma.
"The critic wants us to stop packaging our products altogether, which is absurd." The critic only asked to reduce plastic packaging, so this misrepresents the position: a straw man.

When two speakers disagree, the point at issue is the claim about which they give opposite answers. In "move the festival to summer because the weather is better" versus "keep it in winter because tourists are on holiday", the issue is which season is best.
The best evidence compares like with like: a trial with a control group beats popularity, authority or "other places do it".

deepDiveAspects.title: Irrelevance
deepDiveAspects.content: A statement can be true and still irrelevant; check the link to the conclusion.

deepDiveAspects.title: Principle questions
deepDiveAspects.content: To find the principle behind an argument, generalise its reasoning in one sentence.

solvedExamples.title: Ad hominem
solvedExamples.question: "Dr Rao's report on pollution cannot be trusted because he once failed an examination." What is the fallacy?

steps.title: Move
steps.explanation: Attacks the author, not the report.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: It attacks the person instead of the argument
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The report's evidence is not discussed.

solvedExamples.title: False dilemma
solvedExamples.question: "We must either ban all cars or accept constant traffic jams." What is wrong?
solvedExamples.finalAnswer: It presents only two options when others exist

solvedExamples.title: Evidence
solvedExamples.question: Which is stronger evidence for a fitness app: "a million downloads" or "a controlled trial where users lost 4 kg more than a control group"?

steps.title: Trial
steps.explanation: Shows effect compared with a control.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Find the conclusion, find the move, name the fallacy; for evidence questions prefer controlled comparisons.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling every weak argument a fallacy

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Eliminate options that restate the argument.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Learn the five fallacy labels well.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: The best evidence is specific, comparative and relevant.

easy.question:
Anil: The city should plant more trees because they reduce heat. Bina: That is a poor idea, because trees are expensive.

Bina's reply is weak because it
options: is based on an unreliable survey
does not show that the cost outweighs the benefit Anil mentions
attacks Anil personally
agrees with Anil's main point
easy.correctAnswer: does not show that the cost outweighs the benefit Anil mentions
easy.explanation: A cost is raised, but without showing it exceeds the benefit of cooler streets.

easy.question:
A speaker argues that the library should extend its opening hours.

Which of the following would be irrelevant to the argument?
options: The library's roof was repaired last year.
Many students need a quiet place to study in the evening.
Office workers can only visit after 5 p.m.
Membership has risen by 20% this year.
easy.correctAnswer: The library's roof was repaired last year.
easy.explanation: The roof repair has no bearing on opening hours; the other statements concern demand for evening use.

easy.question:
Meera: The festival should move to the summer, because the weather is better then. Naveen: It should stay in winter, because that is when tourists are on holiday.

The point at issue between Meera and Naveen is
options: whether the weather is better in summer
whether tourists like festivals
whether the festival should be cancelled
which season is best for the festival
easy.correctAnswer: which season is best for the festival
easy.explanation: They give opposite answers about the best season; the weather and tourist claims are their reasons, not the disagreement itself.

intermediate.question:
Dr Rao's report on pollution cannot be trusted because he once failed an examination.

This argument commits the error of
options: attacking the person instead of the evidence
assuming what it sets out to prove
offering only two options
misrepresenting the report
intermediate.correctAnswer: attacking the person instead of the evidence
intermediate.explanation: It dismisses the report because of the author's past, not because of its contents: ad hominem.

intermediate.question:
We must either ban all cars from the city or accept constant traffic jams.

The argument is flawed because it
options: uses a biased sample
attacks the opponent
relies on popularity
ignores other options such as better public transport
intermediate.correctAnswer: ignores other options such as better public transport
intermediate.explanation: It offers only two options when others exist: a false dilemma.

intermediate.question:
Critic: The company should reduce its plastic packaging. Manager: The critic wants us to stop packaging our products altogether, which is absurd.

The manager's reply is flawed because it
options: attacks the critic personally
offers only two options
depends on the popularity of the product
misrepresents the critic's position
intermediate.explanation: The critic asked for a reduction, not an end to packaging: a straw man.

advanced.question:
Speaker 1: Our city's air quality improved after the odd-even car rule began, so the rule works. Speaker 2: In the same period the winds were stronger than in earlier years, and wind clears pollution.

Which of the following would best help decide who is right?
options: The number of cars owned in the first city
The opinions of motorists in the first city
The air quality of a similar city that had the same winds but no odd-even rule
The number of days the rule was in force
advanced.correctAnswer: The air quality of a similar city that had the same winds but no odd-even rule
advanced.explanation: A comparison city with the same winds but no rule separates the effect of the rule from the effect of the wind.

advanced.question:
"Every time I wash my car, it rains, so washing my car causes rain."

Which of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning?
options: All umbrellas keep people dry, so Meena's umbrella keeps her dry.
Every time Meena brings her umbrella, it rains, so Meena's umbrella causes rain.
It rains in monsoon, and this is the monsoon, so it will rain.
Meena brings an umbrella only when rain is forecast.
advanced.correctAnswer: Every time Meena brings her umbrella, it rains, so Meena's umbrella causes rain.
advanced.explanation: Both infer a cause from a repeated coincidence; the other arguments are valid or use different reasoning.

placementStyle.question:
The company should not hire Sam, because he was dismissed from his last job.

Which principle underlies the argument?
options: Everyone deserves a second chance.
A past dismissal is a good reason not to hire someone.
Dismissal is always unfair.
Companies should hire only experienced people.
placementStyle.correctAnswer: A past dismissal is a good reason not to hire someone.
placementStyle.explanation: The argument treats a past dismissal as a sufficient reason against hiring.

placementStyle.question:
An advertisement says: "Our batteries last 20% longer."

Which question would best test this claim?
options: Longer than what?
Who designed the packaging?
How many shops sell the batteries?
What colour are the batteries?
placementStyle.explanation: The claim is meaningless without a comparison, so the first question is "longer than what?".

placementStyle.question:
Two reasons are given for recommending a fitness app. I. It has a million downloads. II. In a 12-week trial, users who followed its plan lost an average of 4 kg more than a control group.

Which of the following is correct?
options: Only reason I is strong evidence
Both reasons are equally strong evidence
Neither reason is relevant to effectiveness
Only reason II is strong evidence of effectiveness
placementStyle.correctAnswer: Only reason II is strong evidence of effectiveness
placementStyle.explanation: Downloads show popularity; the trial compares users with a control group and so measures the effect.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I find the point at issue?
